OffOn Stream on Promising COVID-19 antiviral pill, Paxlovid, in scarce supply, as doctors, patients compete for access Unvaccinated people are often given priority because of a greater risk of dying. ByAnne Flaherty and Soo Rin Kim January 29, 2022, 4:06 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google Dr. Albert Lam, a geriatrician who works with nursing home patients in Palo Alto, California, was excited to be among the first to prescribe the new antiviral pill Paxlovid after one of his patients tested positive for COVID-19. Hailed as a "game-changer" in the pandemic, Paxlovid is a drug made by Pfizer that if taken within five days of being diagnosed reduces the chance of hospitalization and death by 88% for people who are at high risk of severe illness. The treatment has proved so promising that President Joe Biden included it in a Jan. 4 televised speech on the omicron variant, announcing that the first batch had shipped on Christmas Eve. While production would take "months," Biden said it was in "full swing" and promised the drugs were on their way. "The United States has more pills than any other country in the world, and our supply is going to ramp up over the coming months as more of these pills are manufactured," Biden said. Related MORE: GOP governors accuse Biden of controlling the supply of COVID treatments. The alternative could be a bidding war. Lam's patient, a woman in her 80s with a history of cancer, got the drug within 24 hours and responded well. Since then, however, the doctor hasn't been so lucky. President Joe Biden speaks during a meeting of the White House COVID-19 Response Team, Jan. 4 , 2022, in Washington, D.C. Win Mcnamee/Getty Images Whereas nursing homes were first in line to get COVID vaccines last year, Lam now regularly scours a publicly available federal database to see if a Paxlovid prescription pops up near his location. This week, his home state of California got 9,560 doses -- about 24 prescriptions for every 100,000 people. Five weeks after federal regulators approved Paxlovid and began distributing it to states, few people can find it -- omicron's aggressive rise has quickly outstripped supplies. According to an ABC News analysis of federal data on Paxlovid in more than 3,100 U.S. counties, three-quarters didn't have any of the drug on hand as of Jan. 27, and about three-fifths had no access to a provider offering Paxlovid. States are given amounts based on population, but some face more demand than others. Among the states that have the lowest rates of Paxlovid treatment on hand are Alabama, California, Florida, Idaho, New Jersey, New Mexico and Texas, according to data released by the Department of Health and Human Services. Paxlovid, Pfizer's COVID-19 pill, is manufactured in Ascoli, Italy, in this undated handout photo obtained by Reuters, Nov. 16, 2021. Pfizer via Reuters, FILE Race also seems to be a factor in access, at least for now: Urban counties with majority nonwhite population have the lowest average of doses on hand, whereas counties with less than 10% of its population being nonwhite have the highest average of treatments on hand. Scarcity isn't the only problem. Doctors and pharmacists told ABC News the process of obtaining the drug is opaque, even arbitrary. In Nevada, for example, Paxlovid primarily goes to long-term care facilities like nursing homes. But in neighboring California, state officials use a complex formula that factors in rising case numbers with other risk factors. In the District of Columbia, a few Safeway grocery stores are the primary distributors, although city health officials have asked doctors to give priority to high-risk individuals. Dr. Christian Ramers of the Family Health Centers of San Diego, a network of clinics for low-income patients, said his clinic was able to secure its first shipment of 100 treatments of Paxlovid two weeks ago as part of a Biden program aimed at improving health equity. But the staff also had to set up a system, using federal guidelines, to decide who gets the drugs first because there just weren't enough. Often, that's meant prioritizing people who initially refused a vaccination and now are at much greater risk of dying. "The volume has been just mind-blowing for the last three to four weeks -- just absolutely insane," he said. That spike "to us means hundreds to thousands of people vying for about ... 40 to 50 treatment slots per day." For now, he said, the reality is "if you're vaccinated and you're under age 65 and you don't have a medical condition, you're not going to get Paxlovid." Related MORE: How monoclonal antibodies work against omicron variant Adding to the confusion is that many doctors are nervous about prescribing the drug for many high-risk patients because of potentially dangerous interactions with other commonly used medications, including cholesterol-lowering drugs and certain anti-depressants. Advocates say more data should be collected on people in their 80s and 90s. But there aren't a lot of other options. Popular Reads Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say 2 days ago 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police 2 hours ago Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Oct 11 "It is a little disappointing, and it makes me wonder: Could we do more?" said Erin Karara, a pharmacy consultant who works with nursing homes and long-term care facilities. "I mean, we're seeing entire wings of nursing homes or facilities converted to COVID units. ... It's a lot of people affected by it." For its part, both the White House and Pfizer said the drug was never expected to roll out in large numbers right away, in part because of the time it takes to secure raw materials and to scale up manufacturing. The current plan calls for 265,000 courses of treatment in January, gradually ramping up to 10 million by the end of June and 20 million by the end of September. This week, Pfizer told ABC News it plans to increase its production of Paxlovid overall to 120 million courses of treatment globally -- some 3.6 billion pills total. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said producing the drug can't be compared to its COVID vaccine. Boxes of Pfizer's Paxlovid antiviral medication arranged in a warehouse in Shoham, Israel, Jan. 18, 2022. Bloomberg via Getty Images "It is very different, the situation," Bourla said at anindustry conference. "Any decent manufacturer of medicines can make it. But the chemistry, it is complicated, and it takes time to synthesize the active substance." Some conservatives still have been quick to criticize Biden's handling of the rollout, with The Wall Street Journal's editorial board deriding it as "Biden's Operation Snail Speed," writing, "Why didn't it order more treatments sooner?" According to one senior administration official, the White House did everything it could, including promising to Pfizer last July it would spend at least $1 billion on the drugs if it worked. This informal "handshake agreement" was intended to be a powerful incentive for the company, which doesn't use government money to develop new products, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Related MORE: As new variants emerge, US government turns attention to a universal coronavirus vaccine By then, Pfizer had already spent months preparing its supply chain and developing the drug. It agreed to allow the U.S. to receive the world's first shipments. A company official declined to confirm details of private discussions with the White House before the drug became available. "Thanks to this at-risk preparation -- drawing on our deep expertise -- we have already shipped hundreds of thousands of Paxlovid courses in the U.S.," a spokesperson told ABC. "We continue to work quickly to ship courses in accordance with our agreed delivery schedule." COVID-19 antiviral pills, Paxlovid, at a laboratory in Freiburg, Germany. Pfizer/AFP via Getty Images, FILE Two years into the pandemic, doctors still have few ways to treat COVID-19 with vaccines as the most effective option. Treatment options dwindled further this week when federal regulators pulled authorization of two types of monoclonal antibodies that had been widely used in the pandemic, including the kind given to then-President Donald Trump. The antibody cocktails, made by Eli Lilly and Regeneron, were found to be useless against omicron, now 99.9% of all U.S. cases. Two remaining drugs, Remdesivir and Sotrovimab, have to be administered intravenously at a medical facility. Molnupiravir, the new antiviral pill from Merck and Ridgeback Biotherapeutics, found to be 30% effective at preventing hospitalization and death, is authorized only for high-risk patients who can't access other treatments. Related MORE: FDA authorizes Merck pill for COVID-19 treatment That leaves Paxlovid -- if a person can find it and take it early enough, and if the medication doesn't put them at risk because of other drugs they are taking. This week, the Southern Nevada Health District in Las Vegas announced it received 120 prescriptions last week and was willing to offer the medication to anyone older than 12 who is at high risk of COVID and tests positive through their clinic. "If we can identify and treat people early in the course of their illness who otherwise may have ended up in the emergency department or hospital ... we can potentially reduce the impact on our hospital system," said Dr. Cort Lohff, chief medical officer of the public health agency. Lam, the doctor in northern California, said he's hopeful access will improve, particularly for nursing homes and long-term care residents. "Frankly," he added, "I think that if we were able to target those advanced therapeutics for the most at-risk populations, I think we would really make a bigger difference in terms of our death rate." OffOn Stream on Promising COVID-19 antiviral pill, Paxlovid, in scarce supply, as doctors, patients compete for access Unvaccinated people are often given priority because of a greater risk of dying. ByAnne Flaherty and Soo Rin Kim January 29, 2022, 4:06 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google Dr. Albert Lam, a geriatrician who works with nursing home patients in Palo Alto, California, was excited to be among the first to prescribe the new antiviral pill Paxlovid after one of his patients tested positive for COVID-19. Hailed as a "game-changer" in the pandemic, Paxlovid is a drug made by Pfizer that if taken within five days of being diagnosed reduces the chance of hospitalization and death by 88% for people who are at high risk of severe illness. The treatment has proved so promising that President Joe Biden included it in a Jan. 4 televised speech on the omicron variant, announcing that the first batch had shipped on Christmas Eve. While production would take "months," Biden said it was in "full swing" and promised the drugs were on their way. "The United States has more pills than any other country in the world, and our supply is going to ramp up over the coming months as more of these pills are manufactured," Biden said. Related MORE: GOP governors accuse Biden of controlling the supply of COVID treatments. The alternative could be a bidding war. Lam's patient, a woman in her 80s with a history of cancer, got the drug within 24 hours and responded well. Since then, however, the doctor hasn't been so lucky. President Joe Biden speaks during a meeting of the White House COVID-19 Response Team, Jan. 4 , 2022, in Washington, D.C. Win Mcnamee/Getty Images Whereas nursing homes were first in line to get COVID vaccines last year, Lam now regularly scours a publicly available federal database to see if a Paxlovid prescription pops up near his location. This week, his home state of California got 9,560 doses -- about 24 prescriptions for every 100,000 people. Five weeks after federal regulators approved Paxlovid and began distributing it to states, few people can find it -- omicron's aggressive rise has quickly outstripped supplies. According to an ABC News analysis of federal data on Paxlovid in more than 3,100 U.S. counties, three-quarters didn't have any of the drug on hand as of Jan. 27, and about three-fifths had no access to a provider offering Paxlovid. States are given amounts based on population, but some face more demand than others. Among the states that have the lowest rates of Paxlovid treatment on hand are Alabama, California, Florida, Idaho, New Jersey, New Mexico and Texas, according to data released by the Department of Health and Human Services. Paxlovid, Pfizer's COVID-19 pill, is manufactured in Ascoli, Italy, in this undated handout photo obtained by Reuters, Nov. 16, 2021. Pfizer via Reuters, FILE Race also seems to be a factor in access, at least for now: Urban counties with majority nonwhite population have the lowest average of doses on hand, whereas counties with less than 10% of its population being nonwhite have the highest average of treatments on hand. Scarcity isn't the only problem. Doctors and pharmacists told ABC News the process of obtaining the drug is opaque, even arbitrary. In Nevada, for example, Paxlovid primarily goes to long-term care facilities like nursing homes. But in neighboring California, state officials use a complex formula that factors in rising case numbers with other risk factors. In the District of Columbia, a few Safeway grocery stores are the primary distributors, although city health officials have asked doctors to give priority to high-risk individuals. Dr. Christian Ramers of the Family Health Centers of San Diego, a network of clinics for low-income patients, said his clinic was able to secure its first shipment of 100 treatments of Paxlovid two weeks ago as part of a Biden program aimed at improving health equity. But the staff also had to set up a system, using federal guidelines, to decide who gets the drugs first because there just weren't enough. Often, that's meant prioritizing people who initially refused a vaccination and now are at much greater risk of dying. "The volume has been just mind-blowing for the last three to four weeks -- just absolutely insane," he said. That spike "to us means hundreds to thousands of people vying for about ... 40 to 50 treatment slots per day." For now, he said, the reality is "if you're vaccinated and you're under age 65 and you don't have a medical condition, you're not going to get Paxlovid." Related MORE: How monoclonal antibodies work against omicron variant Adding to the confusion is that many doctors are nervous about prescribing the drug for many high-risk patients because of potentially dangerous interactions with other commonly used medications, including cholesterol-lowering drugs and certain anti-depressants. Advocates say more data should be collected on people in their 80s and 90s. But there aren't a lot of other options. Popular Reads Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say 2 days ago 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police 2 hours ago Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Oct 11 "It is a little disappointing, and it makes me wonder: Could we do more?" said Erin Karara, a pharmacy consultant who works with nursing homes and long-term care facilities. "I mean, we're seeing entire wings of nursing homes or facilities converted to COVID units. ... It's a lot of people affected by it." For its part, both the White House and Pfizer said the drug was never expected to roll out in large numbers right away, in part because of the time it takes to secure raw materials and to scale up manufacturing. The current plan calls for 265,000 courses of treatment in January, gradually ramping up to 10 million by the end of June and 20 million by the end of September. This week, Pfizer told ABC News it plans to increase its production of Paxlovid overall to 120 million courses of treatment globally -- some 3.6 billion pills total. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said producing the drug can't be compared to its COVID vaccine. Boxes of Pfizer's Paxlovid antiviral medication arranged in a warehouse in Shoham, Israel, Jan. 18, 2022. Bloomberg via Getty Images "It is very different, the situation," Bourla said at anindustry conference. "Any decent manufacturer of medicines can make it. But the chemistry, it is complicated, and it takes time to synthesize the active substance." Some conservatives still have been quick to criticize Biden's handling of the rollout, with The Wall Street Journal's editorial board deriding it as "Biden's Operation Snail Speed," writing, "Why didn't it order more treatments sooner?" According to one senior administration official, the White House did everything it could, including promising to Pfizer last July it would spend at least $1 billion on the drugs if it worked. This informal "handshake agreement" was intended to be a powerful incentive for the company, which doesn't use government money to develop new products, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Related MORE: As new variants emerge, US government turns attention to a universal coronavirus vaccine By then, Pfizer had already spent months preparing its supply chain and developing the drug. It agreed to allow the U.S. to receive the world's first shipments. A company official declined to confirm details of private discussions with the White House before the drug became available. "Thanks to this at-risk preparation -- drawing on our deep expertise -- we have already shipped hundreds of thousands of Paxlovid courses in the U.S.," a spokesperson told ABC. "We continue to work quickly to ship courses in accordance with our agreed delivery schedule." COVID-19 antiviral pills, Paxlovid, at a laboratory in Freiburg, Germany. Pfizer/AFP via Getty Images, FILE Two years into the pandemic, doctors still have few ways to treat COVID-19 with vaccines as the most effective option. Treatment options dwindled further this week when federal regulators pulled authorization of two types of monoclonal antibodies that had been widely used in the pandemic, including the kind given to then-President Donald Trump. The antibody cocktails, made by Eli Lilly and Regeneron, were found to be useless against omicron, now 99.9% of all U.S. cases. Two remaining drugs, Remdesivir and Sotrovimab, have to be administered intravenously at a medical facility. Molnupiravir, the new antiviral pill from Merck and Ridgeback Biotherapeutics, found to be 30% effective at preventing hospitalization and death, is authorized only for high-risk patients who can't access other treatments. Related MORE: FDA authorizes Merck pill for COVID-19 treatment That leaves Paxlovid -- if a person can find it and take it early enough, and if the medication doesn't put them at risk because of other drugs they are taking. This week, the Southern Nevada Health District in Las Vegas announced it received 120 prescriptions last week and was willing to offer the medication to anyone older than 12 who is at high risk of COVID and tests positive through their clinic. "If we can identify and treat people early in the course of their illness who otherwise may have ended up in the emergency department or hospital ... we can potentially reduce the impact on our hospital system," said Dr. Cort Lohff, chief medical officer of the public health agency. Lam, the doctor in northern California, said he's hopeful access will improve, particularly for nursing homes and long-term care residents. "Frankly," he added, "I think that if we were able to target those advanced therapeutics for the most at-risk populations, I think we would really make a bigger difference in terms of our death rate." SEREMBAN: The Health Ministry expects a slight increase in the number of Covid-19 cases in the next few weeks following the detection of a small wave of infections with the Omicron XBB subvariant in the country. Its caretaker minister, Khairy Jamaluddin, however advised the public not to be alarmed by the development, but to always stay vigilant, as the country was still in transition to the endemic phase. "We have detected the XBB strain in Malaysia, but so far it has not led to an increase in terms of hospital admissions and deaths. That is the most important measurement. "To what extent cases will increase, my officials at the ministry are making a projection based on the infection model we have before and next week I will be able to give a more accurate projection," he told reporters after presenting devices under the Malaysian Family Student Device programme at Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) Seremban campus here, today. It was reported earlier that Singapore's Health Ministry informed that the number of Covid-19 cases in the country had increased since last month, mainly caused by the Omicron XBB subvariant, with the wave of XBB infections expected to peak in mid-November. "The transition to the endemic phase must take into account the mutation of the virus to a new variant, if an unexpected new variant can increase infectivity, effects and symptoms, only then will we review (face mask requirement), but so far it is not necessary," he said. He said the Health Ministry had not introduced additional measures for individuals commuting between Johor Baru and Singapore, but the ministry was constantly monitoring and had been in contact with Singapore's Health Minister Ong Ye Kung regarding the matter. Meanwhile, he said the ministry had sent a proposed standard operating procedure (SOP) to the Election Commission for the 15th General Election (GE15) and no additional measures or restrictions had been introduced. "I see that the situation is under control so we don't want any restrictions. If you want to hold a talk, you are free to do so, but wear a mask in a crowded place. The ministry has given its recommendations to the EC so that voting can be conducted safely, " he said. Earlier, during the handover ceremony, Khairy said digital devices were no longer a luxury, but a necessity as numerous information on courses, research and so forth were available online. analysis.brief_en: The Malaysian Health Ministry has confirmed the detection of the Omicron XBB subvariant, which is expected to cause a slight increase in Covid-19 cases in the coming weeks. However, so far, the strain has not resulted in a significant rise in hospital admissions or deaths. Caretaker Health Minister Khairy Jamaluddin urged the public to remain vigilant but not alarmed, as the country is transitioning to an endemic phase. The ministry is using existing infection models to project the spread of the XBB variant and plans to provide more accurate data next week. Additionally, the ministry has been in communication with Singapore's Health Minister regarding the cross-border spread of the virus, though no additional measures have been introduced for individuals traveling between Malaysia and Singapore. The situation remains under active monitoring, with no explicit risk level communicated at this time.

news.source_body_en: The Malaysian Health Ministry has confirmed the detection of the Omicron XBB subvariant, which is expected to cause a slight increase in Covid-19 cases in the coming weeks. However, so far, the strain has not resulted in a significant rise in hospital admissions or deaths. Caretaker Health Minister Khairy Jamaluddin urged the public to remain vigilant but not alarmed, as the country is transitioning to an endemic phase. The ministry is using existing infection models to project the spread of the XBB variant and plans to provide more accurate data next week. Additionally, the ministry has been in communication with Singapore's Health Minister regarding the cross-border spread of the virus, though no additional measures have been introduced for individuals traveling between Malaysia and Singapore. The situation remains under active monitoring, with no explicit risk level communicated at this time.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 14, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology mRNA-Delivered Bispecific Antibodies Show Promise Against Evolving SARS-CoV-2 Variants by October 14, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 mRNA-Delivered Bispecific Antibodies Show Promise Against Evolving SARS-CoV-2 Variants Study Biology Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram More than five years after the COVID-19 pandemic first reshaped global public health, SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate and evolve, posing a persistent threat to the most vulnerable members of the population. While vaccines have saved countless lives, they depend on a functional immune system to generate protective responses, and this is precisely what many immunocompromised patients cannot mount. For these individuals, antibody therapies delivered directly into the bloodstream have served as a critical line of defense, binding to the virus and neutralizing it before infection can take hold. Yet the virus has repeatedly outmaneuvered these drugs. Each wave of variants, from Alpha through Delta and the many descendants of Omicron, has carried mutations in the viral spike protein that strip away the effectiveness of first-generation monoclonal antibodies, leaving clinicians with fewer and fewer options. A new study published in Science Translational Medicine now describes an engineered solution designed to break this cycle of escape, combining mRNA delivery technology with sophisticated structural protein engineering to create antibodies that constrain the virus’s ability to evade recognition. The research, led by Anna Wec and colleagues, began with a large-scale search for new neutralizing antibodies. Using high-throughput screening approaches, the team isolated several antibody candidates from llamas, animals whose immune systems are well known in the biotechnology field for producing single-domain antibodies, sometimes called nanobodies, that are smaller and structurally distinct from conventional human antibodies. These llama-derived candidates showed the ability to neutralize two of the most immune-evasive Omicron subvariants identified to date, XBB.1.5 and JN.1, both of which carried dense clusters of spike mutations that had disabled most previously authorized antibody therapeutics. The identification of antibodies capable of recognizing these heavily mutated variants provided the raw material for a more ambitious engineering effort aimed at durability rather than just potency. From these lead candidates, the researchers constructed bispecific antibodies, engineered molecules that combine the targeting regions of two different antibodies into a single therapeutic protein. The strategic logic behind bispecific design is straightforward: if a therapeutic antibody binds to two separate sites on the viral spike protein simultaneously, the virus must acquire mutations at both locations at once to escape neutralization. The probability of such a combined mutational event occurring without compromising the virus’s fitness is far lower than the probability of escape from a single-site antibody. In effect, bispecific antibodies raise the genetic barrier to resistance, forcing the virus into a corner where the mutations needed for escape come at a cost to its own replication or transmission. This principle has long been appreciated in antiviral drug design, where combination therapies have proven essential for controlling rapidly evolving pathogens such as HIV. Study Biology Discover more Study Biology Track Biotech Study Chemistry Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care However, bispecific antibodies have historically been difficult and expensive to manufacture. Producing them requires co-expressing two different antibody chains in the same cell and ensuring they assemble correctly into the intended molecule, a process that generates manufacturing complexity and cost far exceeding that of conventional monoclonal antibodies. These burdens have slowed the clinical deployment of bispecific formats, particularly in infectious disease applications where large quantities of drug may be needed and where rapid response to emerging variants is essential. The new study addressed this bottleneck directly by introducing structural modifications that allow multiple bispecific antibodies to be delivered in tandem through a single mRNA construct, sidestepping much of the traditional manufacturing challenge. The mRNA approach represents a conceptual inversion of how antibody therapies have traditionally been produced. Rather than manufacturing antibodies in bioreactors, purifying them, and infusing the finished proteins into patients, mRNA therapy delivers the genetic instructions for the antibodies in the form of messenger RNA. Once the mRNA enters cells, the patients’ own cellular machinery translates the genetic code and produces the therapeutic antibodies in situ, releasing them into the bloodstream. This platform proved its worth during the pandemic in the vaccine context, and its application to antibody delivery offers several advantages: the same lipid nanoparticle manufacturing process can be used for virtually any antibody sequence, new variants can be countered by simply updating the encoded sequence, and multiple antibody specificities can be packaged together in a single formulation. Track Biotech Discover more Read Med Journals Seek Counseling Bioengineering careers guide A key technical hurdle in multiplexed mRNA delivery is ensuring that co-delivered antibody components do not interfere with one another. Antibody heavy chains and light chains from different specificities can mispair when expressed in the same cell, generating a mixture of nonfunctional or unpredictable molecules. The researchers solved this problem through what they describe as orthogonal Fc engineering, a set of structural modifications to the antibody constant region that ensures each antibody component assembles only with its intended partner. This orthogonal design principle, borrowed in spirit from genetic code expansion and synthetic biology, allows several distinct bispecific antibodies to be encoded and expressed simultaneously from a single mRNA dose without cross-reactivity, maximizing the breadth of viral coverage that can be achieved with one therapeutic product. The performance of the engineered platform in laboratory testing was notable. In serum neutralization assays, the mRNA-encoded bispecific antibody cocktail neutralized a broad range of both historical and currently circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants, spanning the evolutionary distance from early pandemic isolates to the latest immune-evasive Omicron descendants. This breadth reflects the combined targeting of multiple conserved and semi-conserved epitopes on the spike protein, a coverage profile that no single conventional antibody has been able to achieve against this virus. In animal studies, the therapy protected mice against infection with the XBB.1.5 variant, providing direct evidence that the mRNA-delivered antibodies reach protective concentrations in vivo and function against a variant that has evaded nearly all previous antibody drugs. Beyond the immediate application to COVID-19, the structural template established in this work has implications that extend across antiviral medicine and beyond. The authors note that the platform may have applications in other therapeutic areas in which broad antigen coverage, resistance to escape, or simultaneous engagement of multiple disease-associated targets is desirable. Rapidly mutating RNA viruses such as influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and HIV all present the same fundamental challenge that SARS-CoV-2 has posed: the target is a moving one, and single-target therapeutics are quickly rendered obsolete. A modular platform in which new antibody combinations can be encoded, updated, and delivered via mRNA offers a path toward therapies that evolve in step with their targets, much as seasonal vaccine formulations are updated each year. The convergence of llama-derived antibody discovery, bispecific engineering, orthogonal assembly design, and mRNA delivery in a single therapeutic platform illustrates how lessons from the pandemic era are being consolidated into next-generation tools. For immunocompromised patients who remain unable to benefit fully from vaccination, the prospect of a durable, broadly neutralizing, and rapidly updatable antibody therapy is clinically significant. While the results reported so far come from serum assays and mouse models, and human clinical testing would be required before any regulatory deployment, the study demonstrates that the escape problem that has plagued antibody therapeutics throughout the pandemic is not an unsolvable one. By designing therapeutics that constrain viral escape rather than merely reacting to it, researchers are shifting the strategic balance in the long-running contest between antiviral drugs and the pathogens they target, offering a template for keeping pace with viruses that refuse to stand still. supplementary_news.content: Company Logo Syndromic multiplex diagnostics can lower costs, improve outcomes and combat Anti Microbial Resistance as Point of Care Testing and Molecular Diagnostics converge. Dublin, Oct. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- "Syndromic Multiplex Diagnostic Markets with COVID-19 Impacts. Strategies and Trends, Forecasts by Syndrome (Respiratory, Sepsis, GI Etc.), by Country, with Market Analysis, Executive Guides and Customization" has been added to ResearchAndMarkets.com's offering. Syndromic multiplex diagnostics are reshaping the infectious disease testing market as healthcare systems seek faster results, more efficient clinical workflows and improved patient outcomes. Accelerated by the COVID pandemic, this transformation is creating new opportunities for diagnostic companies, healthcare providers, laboratories and investors. The report examines the expanding syndromic testing market and evaluates whether its already rapid growth could accelerate further. Market participants are reporting double-digit growth as healthcare organizations increasingly adopt diagnostic platforms capable of supporting timely, targeted clinical decisions. The analysis explores how these technologies may affect established infectious disease testing protocols and the future use of pathogen-specific tests. A central focus is the convergence of Point of Care Testing and Molecular Diagnostics. This combination is gaining market traction by bringing advanced infectious disease testing closer to patients while supporting faster clinical decision-making. The report assesses the potential for syndromic molecular diagnostics to move beyond centralized laboratories and into Physician's Offices, other decentralized care settings and, where appropriate, the Home. The research also considers whether syndromic testing could replace a significant share of frontline infectious disease testing protocols. By identifying multiple relevant pathogens through a more streamlined diagnostic process, these platforms may reduce unnecessary test ordering, shorten the time to actionable results and support more effective treatment selection. The report analyzes the economic and operational factors that could enable broader adoption while addressing the limitations and challenges that may affect market development. Antimicrobial resistance is another important area of analysis. Faster and more comprehensive infectious disease diagnostics can support antimicrobial stewardship by helping clinicians make better-informed treatment decisions. The report reviews how syndromic multiplex testing may contribute to lower costs, improved outcomes and more appropriate use of antimicrobial therapies across healthcare settings. A dedicated section evaluates the extent to which syndromic molecular diagnostics are replacing traditional panel-based ordering of infectious disease tests. It examines available market data, adoption patterns and changing testing practices to provide insight into the scale and pace of this transition. The analysis also considers the continuing role of physicians and laboratory professionals as diagnostic technologies become more automated and widely accessible. Five year market forecasts provide a forward-looking assessment of market size, growth potential and emerging opportunities. Coverage includes key industry issues, competitive trends, adoption drivers, barriers to implementation and the outlook for infectious disease diagnostics. These insights can help organizations assess market positioning, evaluate strategic opportunities and anticipate changes in clinical testing demand. The report is designed to support investment decisions, company valuations, business planning and competitive analysis with current market data and focused industry intelligence. All report data is available in Excel format on request, enabling users to conduct customized analysis, compare market assumptions and integrate the findings into financial or strategic models. For diagnostic manufacturers, investors, laboratories, healthcare organizations and other industry stakeholders, the report provides a concise, evidence-based view of how syndromic multiplex diagnostics are influencing the future of infectious disease testing. supplementary_news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Epidemiology and virological characteristics of the emerging SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 カイン 2026年10月15日 16:43 Epidemiology and virological characteristics of the emerging SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 Epidemiology and virological characteristics of the emerging SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 Original→Epidemiology and virological characteristics of the emerging SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 | bioRxiv Abstract SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally at high levels and to evolve into new variants. SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally at high levels and continues to evolve into new variants. Recently, a new saltation variant harbouring a highly mutated spike protein, PJ.2.1, emerged in North America. Recently, a new variant called "PJ.2.1" with numerous mutations in its spike protein has emerged in North America. Here, we provide a brief epidemiological and virological characterization of PJ.2.1 and cocirculating variants. In this paper, we provide a brief overview of the epidemiological and virological characteristics of PJ.2.1 and other variants circulating in parallel. We report that PJ.2.1 is spreading in the USA, Canada, and Spain and mainly infects individuals aged 60 years and older, as do most other variants, with the exception of BA.3.2, which preferentially infects individuals aged 0-9 years. It was confirmed that PJ.2.1 is spreading in the USA, Canada, and Spain, and is mainly infecting the population aged 60 and older. This is a trend similar to most other variants, but there are exceptions, such as BA.3.2, which preferentially infects the 0-9 age group. PJ.2.1 was less susceptible to inhibition by an antibody against ACE2 than were the other variants, indicating increased ACE2 binding. It was suggested that PJ.2.1 is less susceptible to inhibition by antibodies against ACE2 compared to other variants, indicating an increased binding affinity for ACE2. In contrast, PJ.2.1 did not show augmented evasion of antibodies from vaccinees who had received the LP.8.1-adapted vaccine compared with most other variants analysed. On the other hand, regarding the ability to evade antibodies from individuals who received the LP.8.1-adapted vaccine, no results showed that it was particularly increased in PJ.2.1 compared to most other variants analyzed. These results suggest that augmented ACE2 affinity rather than increased antibody evasion might drive the current, rapid spread of PJ.2.1. From the above results, it is possible that the current rapid spread of PJ.2.1 is driven by an increase in affinity for ACE2, rather than by improved antibody evasion. Introduction SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally and remains responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality. SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally and remains a cause of significant morbidity and mortality. New COVID-19 waves are driven by variants arising through either antigenic drift or shift. New waves of COVID-19 are caused by variants arising through either "antigenic drift" or "antigenic shift." Drift variants differ from their precursors by only a few mutations located mainly in the spike protein, which typically reduce sensitivity to antibody-mediated neutralization. Variants resulting from antigenic drift differ from their parent strains mainly due to a few mutations in the spike protein, which typically reduce sensitivity to antibody-mediated neutralization. Shift variants, also termed saltation variants, are highly mutated viruses thought to have evolved during persistent infections before re-entering global circulation. Variants resulting from antigenic shift (also called "saltation variants") are viruses with numerous mutations, thought to have evolved during persistent infections before re-entering global circulation. As a consequence of the large number of mutations in the spike protein, antibody neutralization may be markedly reduced. Due to the large number of mutations in the spike protein, antibody neutralization may be significantly reduced. A novel saltation variant, PJ.2.1, was identified in May 2026 in Canada and is currently spreading. In May 2026, a new saltation variant, "PJ.2.1," was identified in Canada, and its infection is currently spreading. Here, we present a preliminary epidemiological and virological characterization of PJ.2.1 and cocirculating variants. In this paper, we report preliminary epidemiological and virological characteristics of PJ.2.1 and other variants circulating at the same time. Invivyd and the SPEAR Study Group Announce Initiation of “FLINTLOCK” Phase 2 Study of VYD2311, a Monoclonal Antibody for the Potential Treatment of Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome Invivyd, Inc. Wed, October 14, 2026 at 7:01 AM EDT 13 min read IVVD -7.51% Invivyd, Inc. FLINTLOCK Phase 2 clinical trial will evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and clinical efficacy of high-dose monoclonal antibody VYD2311 in adults aged 18-65 years with Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome, also known as COVID vaccine injury Design includes VYD2311 administered in three doses to assess the safety and potential clinical benefit of VYD2311 treatment versus placebo over 90 days VYD2311 has demonstrated high in vitro antiviral potency across all SARS-CoV-2 variants tested from original Wuhan through contemporary Omicron variants FLINTLOCK is part of Invivyd's broader REVOLUTION clinical program for VYD2311, including DECLARATION and LIBERTY Millions of individuals continue to live with persistent and debilitating symptoms of Long COVID, underscoring the significant unmet need for development of effective treatment options NEW HAVEN, Conn., Oct. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Invivyd, Inc. (Nasdaq: IVVD) and the SPEAR Study Group today announced the initiation of FLINTLOCK, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and clinical efficacy of high-dose monoclonal antibody VYD2311 in individuals with Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome (PVS), also known as COVID vaccine injury. "Long COVID continues to be a significant challenge for millions of Americans. It is a disease state characterized by persistent and debilitating symptoms impacting multiple systems across the human body, including immune dysfunction, cardiovascular issues, respiratory challenges, nervous system dysfunction, pain, and other health issues that can impact a person's day-to-day life," noted David Putrino, Ph.D., Nash Family Director of the Cohen Center for Recovery from Complex Chronic Illness at Mount Sinai and Founding Member of the SPEAR Study Group. "We are excited to take the next step in advancing this potential therapeutic option for patients living with Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome, a diagnosis which has received very little attention." The Phase 2 FLINTLOCK clinical trial includes the following study features: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, proof-of-concept study Tests Invivyd's monoclonal antibody VYD2311, an investigational monoclonal antibody that has been demonstrated to be pharmaceutically active against all SARS-CoV-2 variants tested to date from current variants back to original Wuhan variants High-dose initial intravenous (IV) infusion of VYD2311 followed by monthly intramuscular (IM) injections at days 30 and 60 with total dose targeted at 10x the prophylactic dose of VYD2311 assessed in DECLARATION and LIBERTY, while still below doses already assessed with a positive initial safety profile in VYD2311 first-in-human testing (LINK) Inclusion criteria designed to enroll adults aged 18-65 years with confirmed Long COVID or PVS; criteria include having at least 2 persistent symptoms after a COVID-19 infection or following COVID-19 vaccine injury Clinical efficacy evaluations include functional performance tests consistent across prior studies of Long COVID and other infection-associated chronic conditions and illnesses, through Day 90 Assessment of the safety and tolerability of VYD2311 based on the incidence, severity, causality, and outcome of treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and hypersensitivity reactions through Day 90, as well as evaluation of the pharmacokinetics of VYD2311 by measuring serum concentrations through Day 90 Initial data expected in mid-2027. Story Continues "Both Long COVID and COVID PVS may share the inflammatory presence of persistent SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in the underlying disease processes, and so we are bringing to bear our pharmacology that is specifically directed against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein target in large quantities," said Marc Elia, Chairman and CEO of Invivyd. "Previous Long COVID antiviral therapeutic efforts have been limited by use of short course therapies that may not adequately inhibit viral replication, or by the use of monoclonal antibody candidates that lacked activity against many known and circulating clinical variants. However, given anecdotal independent case reports of highly active monoclonal antibodies generating clinical improvements in Long COVID patients, including with our current monoclonal antibody medicine PEMGARDA® (pemivibart), we are looking forward to advancing FLINTLOCK and potentially bringing forward a therapeutic option for the benefit of people suffering from Long COVID." Further details on the FLINTLOCK Phase 2 Long COVID trial of VYD2311 will be posted near-term to www.clinicaltrials.gov. PEMGARDA® (pemivibart) is not authorized or approved for the treatment of Long COVID or PVS. About VYD2311 VYD2311 is a novel monoclonal antibody (mAb) candidate being developed for COVID-19 to continue to address the urgent need for new prophylactic and therapeutic options. The pharmacokinetic profile and antiviral potency of VYD2311 may offer the ability to deliver clinically meaningful titer levels through more patient-friendly means such as an intramuscular route of administration. VYD2311 was engineered using Invivyd's proprietary integrated technology platform and is the product of serial molecular evolution designed to generate an antibody optimized for neutralizing contemporary virus lineages. VYD2311 leverages the same antibody backbone as pemivibart, Invivyd's investigational mAb granted emergency use authorization in the U.S. for the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of symptomatic COVID-19 in certain immunocompromised patients, and adintrevimab, Invivyd's investigational mAb that has a robust safety data package and demonstrated clinically meaningful results in global Phase 2/3 clinical trials for the prevention and treatment of COVID-19. About FLINTLOCK FLINTLOCK is a Phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, proof-of-concept study is being conducted to investigate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, clinical activity, immunogenicity, and SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody response of VYD2311. VYD2311 will be administered first as a loading dose via intravenous infusion on Day 1 followed by additional intramuscular injections on Day 30 and Day 60 in adults aged 18-65 years with a confirmed diagnosis of Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome (PVS), with two or more symptoms, with or without SARS-CoV-2 spike antigen that are present ≥6 months after having a COVID-19 infection or vaccination. Total enrollment of the trial is approximately 130 participants. About DECLARATION DECLARATION is a Phase 3, randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate VYD2311 efficacy and safety in prevention of symptomatic COVID in a broad population of participants including adults and adolescents both with and without risk factors for progression to severe COVID-19 at three months. Participants will receive either a single dose or monthly doses of VYD2311, each administered via intramuscular injection, compared to placebo. Total enrollment of the trial is approximately 2,400 participants. About LIBERTY LIBERTY is a Phase 3, randomized, double-blind study to evaluate the safety, serum virus neutralizing antibody responses, and pharmacokinetics of VYD2311, an mRNA COVID vaccine, and co-administered VYD2311 with an mRNA COVID vaccine. Total enrollment of the trial was approximately 210 participants. About PEMGARDA PEMGARDA® (pemivibart) is a half-life extended investigational monoclonal antibody (mAb). PEMGARDA was engineered from adintrevimab, Invivyd's investigational mAb that has a robust safety data package and provided evidence of clinical efficacy in global Phase 2/3 clinical trials for the prevention and treatment of COVID-19. PEMGARDA has demonstrated in vitro neutralizing activity against major SARS-CoV-2 variants, including JN.1, KP.3.1.1, XEC, LP.8.1 and XFG. PEMGARDA targets the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein receptor binding domain (RBD), thereby inhibiting virus attachment to the human ACE2 receptor on host cells. PEMGARDA (pemivibart) injection (4500 mg), for intravenous use is an investigational mAb that has not been approved, but has been authorized for emergency use by the U.S. FDA under an EUA for the pre-exposure prophylaxis (prevention) of COVID-19 in adults and adolescents (12 years of age and older weighing at least 40 kg) who have moderate-to-severe immune compromise due to certain medical conditions or receipt of certain immunosuppressive medications or treatments and are unlikely to mount an adequate immune response to COVID-19 vaccination. Recipients should not be currently infected with or have had a known recent exposure to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2. PEMGARDA is not authorized for use for the treatment of COVID-19, Long COVID, or COVID-19 Post-Vaccination Syndrome, or for post-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19. Pre-exposure prophylaxis with PEMGARDA is not a substitute for vaccination in individuals for whom COVID-19 vaccination is recommended. Individuals for whom COVID-19 vaccination is recommended, including individuals with moderate-to-severe immune compromise who may derive benefit from COVID-19 vaccinations, should receive COVID-19 vaccination. In individuals who have recently received a COVID-19 vaccine, PEMGARDA should be administered at least 2 weeks after vaccination. Pre-exposure prophylaxis with PEMGARDA is not a substitute for vaccination in individuals for whom COVID-19 vaccination is recommended. Individuals for whom COVID-19 vaccination is recommended, including individuals with moderate-to-severe immune compromise who may derive benefit from COVID-19 vaccinations, should receive COVID-19 vaccination. In individuals who have recently received a COVID-19 vaccine, PEMGARDA should be administered at least 2 weeks after vaccination. supplementary_news.content: FLINTLOCK Phase 2 clinical trial will evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and clinical efficacy of high-dose monoclonal antibody VYD2311 in adults aged 18-65 years with Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome, also known as COVID vaccine injury - Design includes VYD2311 administered in three doses to assess the safety and potential clinical benefit of VYD2311 treatment versus placebo over 90 days - VYD2311 has demonstrated high in vitro antiviral potency across all SARS-CoV-2 variants tested from original Wuhan through contemporary Omicron variants - FLINTLOCK is part of Invivyd’s broader REVOLUTION clinical program for VYD2311, including DECLARATION and LIBERTY - Millions of individuals continue to live with persistent and debilitating symptoms of Long COVID, underscoring the significant unmet need for development of effective treatment options NEW HAVEN, Conn., Oct. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Invivyd, Inc. (Nasdaq: IVVD) and the SPEAR Study Group today announced the initiation of FLINTLOCK, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and clinical efficacy of high-dose monoclonal antibody VYD2311 in individuals with Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome (PVS), also known as COVID vaccine injury. "Long COVID continues to be a significant challenge for millions of Americans. It is a disease state characterized by persistent and debilitating symptoms impacting multiple systems across the human body, including immune dysfunction, cardiovascular issues, respiratory challenges, nervous system dysfunction, pain, and other health issues that can impact a person’s day-to-day life,” noted David Putrino, Ph.D., Nash Family Director of the Cohen Center for Recovery from Complex Chronic Illness at Mount Sinai and Founding Member of the SPEAR Study Group. "We are excited to take the next step in advancing this potential therapeutic option for patients living with Long COVID or Post-Vaccination Syndrome, a diagnosis which has received very little attention.” The Phase 2 FLINTLOCK clinical trial includes the following study features: - Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, proof-of-concept study - Tests Invivyd’s monoclonal antibody VYD2311, an investigational monoclonal antibody that has been demonstrated to be pharmaceutically active against all SARS-CoV-2 variants tested to date from current variants back to original Wuhan variants - High-dose initial intravenous (IV) infusion of VYD2311 followed by monthly intramuscular (IM) injections at days 30 and 60 with total dose targeted at 10x the prophylactic dose of VYD2311 assessed in DECLARATION and LIBERTY, while still below doses already assessed with a positive initial safety profile in VYD2311 first-in-human testing (LINK) - Inclusion criteria designed to enroll adults aged 18-65 years with confirmed Long COVID or PVS; criteria include having at least 2 persistent symptoms after a COVID-19 infection or following COVID-19 vaccine injury - Clinical efficacy evaluations include functional performance tests consistent across prior studies of Long COVID and other infection-associated chronic conditions and illnesses, through Day 90 - Assessment of the safety and tolerability of VYD2311 based on the incidence, severity, causality, and outcome of treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and hypersensitivity reactions through Day 90, as well as evaluation of the pharmacokinetics of VYD2311 by measuring serum concentrations through Day 90 - Initial data expected in mid-2027. "Both Long COVID and COVID PVS may share the inflammatory presence of persistent SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in the underlying disease processes, and so we are bringing to bear our pharmacology that is specifically directed against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein target in large quantities,” said Marc Elia, Chairman and CEO of Invivyd. "Previous Long COVID antiviral therapeutic efforts have been limited by use of short course therapies that may not adequately inhibit viral replication, or by the use of monoclonal antibody candidates that lacked activity against many known and circulating clinical variants. However, given anecdotal independent case reports of highly active monoclonal antibodies generating clinical improvements in Long COVID patients, including with our current monoclonal antibody medicine PEMGARDA® (pemivibart), we are looking forward to advancing FLINTLOCK and potentially bringing forward a therapeutic option for the benefit of people suffering from Long COVID.” Further details on the FLINTLOCK Phase 2 Long COVID trial of VYD2311 will be posted near-term to www.clinicaltrials.gov. PEMGARDA® (pemivibart) is not authorized or approved for the treatment of Long COVID or PVS. About VYD2311 VYD2311 is a novel monoclonal antibody (mAb) candidate being developed for COVID-19 to continue to address the urgent need for new prophylactic and therapeutic options. The pharmacokinetic profile and antiviral potency of VYD2311 may offer the ability to deliver clinically meaningful titer levels through more patient-friendly means such as an intramuscular route of administration. VYD2311 was engineered using Invivyd’s proprietary integrated technology platform and is the product of serial molecular evolution designed to generate an antibody optimized for neutralizing contemporary virus lineages. VYD2311 leverages the same antibody backbone as pemivibart, Invivyd’s investigational mAb granted emergency use authorization in the U.S. for the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of symptomatic COVID-19 in certain immunocompromised patients, and adintrevimab, Invivyd’s investigational mAb that has a robust safety data package and demonstrated clinically meaningful results in global Phase 2/3 clinical trials for the prevention and treatment of COVID-19. About FLINTLOCK FLINTLOCK is a Phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, proof-of-concept study is being conducted to investigate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, clinical activity, immunogenicity, and SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody response of VYD2311. Total enrollment of the trial is approximately 130 participants. About DECLARATION DECLARATION is a Phase 3, randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate VYD2311 efficacy and safety in prevention of symptomatic COVID in a broad population of participants including adults and adolescents both with and without risk factors for progression to severe COVID-19 at three months. Participants will receive either a single dose or monthly doses of VYD2311, each administered via intramuscular injection, compared to placebo. Total enrollment of the trial is approximately 2,400 participants. What parents should know By: Victoria Brown, Dalin Clark Fall and winter mark the peak season for common respiratory infections such as respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV; influenza; and the common cold. These illnesses — along with COVID-19, which tends to peak at similar times — often begin with similar symptoms, so telling them apart can be tricky, especially when the beginning of cold and flu season can be the tail end of seasonal allergies. Ann Sheehan, MSU College of Nursing and MSU Health Care. Courtesy photo. Ann Sheehan, assistant dean for faculty practice and associate professor at MSU’s College of Nursing, has been a pediatric nurse practitioner for more than 20 years. She currently helps families at MSU Health Care Pediatrics make informed decisions about children’s health Here, Sheehan provides insights about how to determine a child’s sickness, why it’s important to differentiate the illnesses, and what can speed recovery. Some symptoms of common illnesses look the same. How can parents tell them apart? Figuring out whether your child has COVID-19, the flu, RSV or the common cold is important because some of these illnesses can cause serious complications in certain children. COVID-19 has a higher risk of severe or long-term health effects, including long COVID, but others are not harmless. The flu can cause significant illness and hospitalization, and RSV can be especially serious for infants, young children and those with chronic health conditions. All four of these illnesses spread easily. Keeping children home when they are sick helps reduce that spread, protecting vulnerable classmates and school staff. Colds are caused by a variety of viruses, which is why they are so common. Frequent cold symptoms include coughing, sneezing, sore throat and a runny nose. These symptoms are generally mild and usually improve on their own within about seven to 10 days. COVID-19, on the other hand, is caused by a single virus called severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, or SARS-CoV-2. The symptoms of COVID-19 tend to last longer — seven to 14 days, with some lingering for three to four weeks. Beyond common cold symptoms like a cough, sore throat and runny nose, people sick with COVID-19 often have body aches, shortness of breath and difficulty breathing, headache, fatigue, fever and loss of taste and/or smell. Signs that often differentiate COVID-19 are stomach symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea. Not all children experience these symptoms, but they are not associated with the common cold. The symptoms of the flu, caused by the influenza A or B virus, tend to come on very quickly, unlike the gradual onset of a cold or COVID-19. Symptoms last about three to seven days, and they’re very similar to those of COVID-19, except they don’t usually include loss of taste or smell. RSV symptoms also align with those of a cold but include a decreased appetite. Also, RSV affects the lungs and can lead to serious lung infections and hospitalization, especially for infants and toddlers. The symptoms can last three to four weeks. When should parents keep their kids at home from school? If your child has symptoms that could be one of these viruses, keeping them home from school is a good idea. It helps protect other children and school staff from becoming ill. A general rule of thumb for making the call is to consider whether your child can comfortably participate in classroom activities. If the answer is yes, then it’s likely fine to send them to school. But if they’ve had a fever in the past 24 hours, or have diarrhea, nausea or vomiting, it’s best that they stay home and rest. The American Academy of Pediatrics notes that children with certain medical conditions, including obesity and diabetes, immune system deficiencies and complex medical conditions, may be more likely to become seriously ill if they contract COVID-19, RSV or the flu. Are COVID-19 tests helpful for diagnosing illness at home? It’s often impossible to tell if a child has COVID-19 based on symptoms alone. A home COVID-19 test can be a useful tool if, for example, your child has some of the typical symptoms or was exposed to someone with COVID-19 — or if your child has a chronic medical condition that puts them at high risk of complications. A positive result is reliable, but a negative result does not completely rule out a COVID-19 infection. That could be because you made an error in following the testing instructions or because there’s not enough virus present to turn the test positive. If the test is negative and symptoms remain, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends retesting in 48 hours or having your healthcare provider order a PCR test. What vaccines are recommended for children? The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends flu vaccinations for all children over the age of 6 months, unless a child has a medical reason not to receive it. The group recommends that children ages 6 to 23 months old, and children ages 2 to 18 who have a higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19, get a COVID-19 vaccine. A study published in December 2025 supports this recommendation. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the CDC also recommend that infants be immunized against RSV based on certain criteria. It’s important to know that children can still become infected with the viruses that cause these illnesses after getting these shots. However, once a child is vaccinated against flu or COVID-19, their immune system recognizes the virus and responds more effectively. And the antibodies used to immunize infants against RSV directly protect them from illness. Not only do these interventions reduce your child’s risk of getting severely ill and being hospitalized if they get one of these viruses, but they also reduce the number of school days your child is likely to miss. When should a parent involve a healthcare professional? Whichever respiratory infection your child has, unless they are at high risk for serious complications, symptoms can usually be managed at home. For most children, there’s no need to seek medical care for every cough and runny nose, even if their COVID-19 test is positive. Most children recover from these viruses without complications. However, some symptoms may indicate a more serious illness and should not be ignored. You know your child best; if their fever does not come down with medication, they are having trouble eating and drinking, or if they are having difficulty breathing, seek medical care. Additionally, caregivers with children who have underlying medical conditions or other risk factors should contact their healthcare provider when children first experience symptoms so they can get treatment if needed. A retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary academic center in Germany examined more than 2,000 adults hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure between March 2020 and December 2024, and found that those who also tested positive for the coronavirus died in the hospital at rates substantially higher than their uninfected counterparts. The findings, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, add to a growing body of evidence that viral respiratory infections can tip vulnerable cardiac patients into lethal territory. The research team, led by investigators at Ruhr University Bochum’s Knappschaft Kliniken University Hospital, analyzed records from 2,002 adults treated for acute decompensated heart failure, a condition in which the heart suddenly cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s demands, causing fluid buildup in the lungs and tissues. Among these patients, 246 individuals, or 12.3 percent, had laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection detected by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction during their hospital stay. This molecular diagnostic technique amplifies and detects viral RNA, providing both a yes-or-no answer about infection and, through the cycle threshold value, an indirect gauge of how much virus a patient is carrying. The raw numbers were stark. Patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection died in the hospital at a rate of 32.5 percent, compared with 20.6 percent among those without the infection. Intensive care unit admission was also more frequent in the infected group, at 61.4 percent versus 50.7 percent, and the need for invasive mechanical ventilation, in which a breathing tube and ventilator take over the work of the lungs, was nearly three times as common, affecting 6.5 percent of infected patients against 2.4 percent of uninfected ones. All of these differences reached statistical significance, with p values at or below 0.002. Book Care Services Discover more Monitor Vitals Check Symptoms infections Infection Infectious Diseases Because raw comparisons between groups can be distorted by differences in age, comorbidities, and disease severity, the researchers applied multivariable regression models that adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. Even after this statistical correction, SARS-CoV-2 infection remained independently associated with in-hospital mortality, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.63 and a p value of 0.0002. An adjusted odds ratio above 2 means that, holding other factors constant, infected patients had more than two and a half times the odds of dying during their hospitalization. The infection also remained independently linked to ICU admission, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.79, and to invasive mechanical ventilation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.84. Find Treatments The burden of infection extended beyond survival and organ support. Hospitalized heart failure patients who also carried SARS-CoV-2 spent significantly longer in the hospital and in the intensive care unit. After adjustment, infection was associated with an additional 9.23 days of hospital stay and an additional 7.85 days of ICU stay, both statistically robust findings. In a condition where timely decongestion and bed capacity are critical, such prolonged stays represent not only worse outcomes for individual patients but also meaningful strain on healthcare resources, particularly during periods when respiratory viruses circulate widely in the community. One of the more technically interesting aspects of the study involved the use of cycle threshold values as surrogate markers of viral burden. In RT-qPCR testing, the cycle threshold, or Ct value, refers to the number of amplification cycles needed before viral RNA becomes detectable. Lower Ct values indicate that less amplification was required, which in turn suggests a higher concentration of virus in the sampled material. The researchers therefore reasoned that Ct values could serve as a rough proxy for how heavily infected each patient was at the time of testing. Among the 246 infected patients, the analysis revealed that lower median Ct values were associated with higher in-hospital mortality, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.89 per Ct unit and a p value of 0.0338. Because the odds ratio is below 1, each unit decrease in Ct value, corresponding to an increase in viral burden, was linked to greater odds of death. Lower minimum Ct values were also associated with longer hospital stays, with an adjusted beta of minus 0.44 days per Ct unit and a p value of 0.0359. Taken together, these findings suggest that patients with higher viral loads fared worse, raising the possibility that viral burden could help stratify mortality risk within this already vulnerable population. Book Care Services Discover more infection Study Biology Study Anatomy Book Care Services Read Med Journals The authors themselves urge caution in interpreting these viral load findings. Cycle threshold values are imperfect surrogate markers of viral burden because they depend on sampling technique, specimen type, timing of testing relative to infection onset, and the specific PCR assay used. A nasal swab taken poorly or late in the course of infection can yield a high Ct value even in a heavily infected patient. The researchers explicitly describe the Ct-based associations as hypothesis-generating and call for prospective validation in future studies before any clinical decision-making relies on viral load measurements in this setting. Interestingly, the study found that the heart failure phenotype itself, meaning whether patients had reduced, mildly reduced, or preserved ejection fraction, and whether they were receiving guideline-directed medical therapy before admission, showed no consistent associations with major in-hospital outcomes. This suggests that the viral infection, rather than the specific characteristics of the underlying cardiac disease or its chronic treatment, was the dominant modifiable factor driving worse outcomes during hospitalization. In other words, the acute viral insult appeared to overwhelm the prognostic influence of chronic heart failure characteristics. The clinical implications of this work are considerable. Acute decompensated heart failure patients represent a clinically vulnerable population in whom respiratory infections have long been recognized as dangerous triggers of decompensation. This study quantifies that danger in the specific context of SARS-CoV-2, showing that concomitant infection roughly doubles the adjusted odds of in-hospital death and dramatically extends length of stay. For clinicians, the findings argue for vigilant screening for SARS-CoV-2 in heart failure admissions during periods of viral circulation, for aggressive monitoring of infected patients, and for continued efforts at vaccination and infection prevention in this high-risk group. For researchers, the viral burden signal points toward a future where quantitative PCR results might do more than confirm infection, potentially helping to identify which heart failure patients need the most intensive care.
